about: Answer key for eval/the_relay_20_evaluation_questions.txt. Questions written by the author. This key was DRAFTED BY THE ASSISTANT from the parsed paper text (data/corpus/blocks.jsonl) on 2026-11-10 and must be checked by the author: set verified=true per question after checking it against the PDF.

grading_rule.correct: Answerable question: EVERY required point is present and right, and each claim carries a citation to a passage that supports it (the cite need only match one of the listed acceptable cites for that point).
grading_rule.wrong: Answerable question: any required point missing, any stated fact wrong (including a forbidden value from 'traps'), or a claim cited to a passage that does not support it. Unanswerable question: anything other than a refusal, i.e. the asked quantity is given or guessed.
grading_rule.refused_correctly: Unanswerable question: the answer says the three papers do not establish the asked information and gives no value for it. Adjacent facts may be mentioned only if cited and explicitly framed as not answering the question.
grading_rule.refused_wrongly: Answerable question: the system refuses or says the papers do not cover it.

cite_format: PAPER §section | PAPER Table N | PAPER Figure N | PAPER Abstract, with PAPER in {AIAYN, MOSHI, HNET}

required.point: For large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude
This pushes the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients
Dot products are scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k) to counteract this

optional: Footnote: if q and k components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, q·k has mean 0 and variance d_k
Without scaling, additive attention outperforms dot-product attention for larger d_k
traps: The paper says the authors 'suspect' this; stating it as proven is acceptable but should not add reasons the paper does not give

required.point: Encoder self-attention: queries, keys and values all come from the output of the previous encoder layer; each position attends to all positions
Decoder self-attention: each position attends only to positions up to and including itself, enforced by masking (setting to -inf) illegal connections in the softmax input
Encoder-decoder attention: queries from the previous decoder layer, keys and values from the encoder output; every decoder position attends over all input positions
Masking prevents leftward information flow to preserve the auto-regressive property: with output embeddings offset by one, predictions for position i depend only on known outputs at positions < i

optional: Figure 2 shows the mask inside scaled dot-product attention

required.point: Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks; same dimension d_model so they can be summed
They use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies (PE(pos,2i)=sin(pos/10000^(2i/d_model)), PE(pos,2i+1)=cos(...)); wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π
Learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results (Table 3 row (E))
Sinusoidal was chosen because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen in training

optional: Hypothesis: lets the model attend by relative position, since PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos)
Table 3 row (E): PPL 4.92, BLEU 25.7 vs base 4.92 / 25.8
traps: The extrapolation reason is a 'may allow', not a demonstrated result

required.point: N = 6 layers (encoder and decoder each)
d_model = 512
h = 8 heads
d_k = 64 and d_v = 64
100K training steps

optional: P_drop = 0.1, ε_ls = 0.1, dev PPL 4.92, dev BLEU 25.8, 65M params
traps: Big-model values must not appear as the answer: d_model 1024, d_ff 4096, h 16, P_drop 0.3, 300K steps, 213M params
'Table 3' exists in all three papers (MOSHI Table 3 is a Mimi ablation, HNET Table 3 is HellaSwag robustness)

required.point: Limitation 1, latency: it compounds along the pipeline's components, giving a global latency of several seconds (vs a few hundred ms in natural conversation)
Limitation 2, text bottleneck: understanding and generation happen in text, so non-written information (paralinguistics such as emotion and accent, non-speech audio) is lost
Limitation 3, turn-based modeling: assumes well-defined single-speaker segments, so it cannot model interruptions, overlapping speech and backchanneling
Moshi casts dialogue as speech-to-speech generation in the audio domain on top of a text LLM backbone (Helium), removing the text bottleneck
Streaming hierarchical architecture with theoretical latency 160 ms (200 ms in practice)
Multi-stream modeling of its own and the user's audio removes the speaker-turn concept, allowing overlap and interruptions

optional: Overlapping speech is 10 to 20% of spoken time
Natural conversation average response time 230 ms across 10 languages

required.point: The two audio streams are Moshi's own speech and the user's speech
The acoustic delay is applied to both streams and they are concatenated into the jointly modeled multi-sequence
There are no explicit turn boundaries: the model always listens and always generates (speech or silence), i.e. full-duplex
At inference Moshi's stream is sampled while the user's predicted stream is replaced by the real user audio
Because there is no speaker-turn segmentation, overlap and interruptions can be modeled

optional: Predicting the user stream too enables simulated dialogues for offline evaluation
Total K = 2Q+1 = 17 streams including the text stream
traps: The text (Inner Monologue) stream is only for Moshi's speech, not the user's

required.point: Mimi is an autoencoder (SeaNet with Transformers) with a residual vector quantization bottleneck: 24 kHz audio to 12.5 Hz latents, Q = 8 quantizers with codebook size 2048
Semantic information is distilled from WavLM into the first quantizer level using a cosine distance
Split RVQ: distillation into a single RVQ's first level hurt audio quality, so semantic information goes into a plain VQ and acoustic information into a 7-level RVQ in parallel, with outputs summed
All convolutions are causal, so Mimi encodes and decodes in streaming fashion: an 80 ms frame yields a latent step that decodes to 80 ms of audio, which makes real-time generation possible

optional: Bitrate 1.1 kbps
Quantization applied only 50% of the time during training
Non-causal pooling of WavLM targets is fine because it is only used in training
traps: The latent is 512-d but projected to 256-d before RVQ

required.point: Inner Monologue: Moshi also models the text of its own speech as a time-aligned text stream inserted as a prefix to the semantic tokens
Alignment: Whisper word-level timestamps are mapped to the 12.5 Hz frames, with PAD and EPAD special tokens filling the gaps between words
It provides scaffolding that increases the linguistic quality of generated speech
Delay controls which modality decides content: audio ahead of text (sample only text with real audio) gives streaming ASR; text ahead of audio gives streaming TTS

optional: Padding tokens are about 65% of text tokens in English conversational speech
The user's speech is not transcribed

required.point: Depth Transformer model dimension 1024
Depth Transformer MLP dimension 4096
Depth Transformer 16 heads
Depth Transformer 6 layers
Audio cardinality 2048
Frame rate 12.5 Hz

traps: Temporal Transformer values must not appear as the answer: model dim 4096, MLP 11264, 32 heads, 32 layers
Text cardinality is 32000, not the audio cardinality

required.point: Encoder networks process the raw (byte-level) input sequence
The chunking layer (routing module + downsampler) compresses the sequence into fewer vectors using dynamically learned boundaries
The main network processes the compressed sequence and can itself be an H-Net, giving recursive multi-stage hierarchies
The dechunking layer (smoothing module + upsampler) restores the original resolution, combined with a residual Linear(x) from the encoder side
Decoder networks process the dechunked sequence back at the original resolution to produce outputs

optional: Inspired by U-Net, but with dynamic rather than fixed-size pooling
Components are stacks of sequence-mixing layers such as Transformers or SSMs

required.point: Routing module: cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs; q_t = W_q x_t, k_t = W_k x_t, p_t = ½(1 − cos(q_t, k_{t−1})), with p_1 = 1
Low similarity at a contextual or semantic shift gives a high boundary probability; boundary indicator b_t = 1 if p_t ≥ 0.5
Downsampler: keeps the vectors where b_t = 1 and discards those where b_t = 0 (direct selection, chosen over mean/max pooling and cross-attention)
The boundary probabilities are compressed the same way and passed to the dechunking layer

optional: Smoothing module (EMA) makes boundaries differentiable during training
traps: The question's 'preserving important information' has no separate mechanism in the downsampler; the paper's reason is selecting boundary-marked vectors for simplicity and effectiveness

required.point: Large: BPE Transformer average 53.3 vs H-Net (2-stage) 55.5
XL: BPE Transformer average 55.5 vs H-Net (2-stage) 58.2
H-Net (2-stage) outperforms the tokenized baseline at both scales (the text states +2.2% at Large and +2.6% at XL)
The Large H-Net (2-stage) matches the average downstream performance of the XL BPE Transformer

optional: H-Net (2-stage) achieves the highest performance across most tasks
traps: Self-contradiction: §3.1 says +2.6% at XL, but Table 2 gives 58.2 − 55.5 = 2.7. Either is acceptable if attributed correctly; claiming the text says 2.7 is wrong
The table labels the baseline 'Transformer (Token)'; the text calls it the BPE Transformer

required.point: Positional encoding solves the lack of order information in a model with no recurrence or convolution: fixed sinusoids of position are added to the embeddings
Dynamic chunking learns content- and context-dependent segmentation end-to-end, replacing tokenization, and compresses the sequence into chunks

Contrast: positional encoding is fixed (not learned), depends only on position, and leaves sequence length unchanged; dynamic chunking is learned, depends on content (similarity of adjacent representations), and changes sequence length

optional: Learned positional embeddings performed about the same (AIAYN Table 3 (E))
DC allocates compute by compressing low-information regions
traps: Neither paper compares the two mechanisms; every comparative claim must rest on cited facts from each paper

required.point: Causal masking enforces that each output position depends only on earlier positions (positions < i), preserving the auto-regressive property
Moshi's acoustic delay: a delay of 1 or 2 steps between semantic and acoustic tokens, which gave more stable, higher-quality generation and lets the Temporal Transformer model their inter-dependence
Moshi's text–audio delay decides which modality determines content, giving streaming ASR (audio ahead) or TTS (text ahead)
Moshi remains autoregressive over time steps: the Temporal Transformer conditions on previous steps

optional: The delay reduces dependencies between sub-sequences at the same step, so a weaker model can approximate the joint distribution

required.point: Moshi: the Temporal Transformer models the time axis, mapping past steps to a context vector z_s; the smaller Depth Transformer models the K sub-sequences (codebooks/streams) within one step, conditioned on z_s
Moshi's problem: flattening the codebooks would need about 100 steps per second (30,000 for 5 minutes), which is computationally costly and incompatible with streaming
H-Net: encoder, then chunking that compresses the sequence length with learned boundaries, then the main network on fewer vectors, then dechunking back to the original resolution; stages can nest
H-Net's problem: replace fixed tokenization with learned end-to-end segmentation and allocate compute by compressing low-information regions
Contrast: Moshi decomposes the per-step depth (codebook) axis, while H-Net decomposes along sequence length

optional: Both are cited as RQ-Transformer / hierarchical relatives (Moshi notes a similar approach was suggested for byte-level modeling)
